```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 144
)
library(suppose)
```

Suppose helps you keep a scientific question, its assumptions, and its revisions
in one inspectable record. This guide takes about five minutes and needs no AI
account. Install ggplot2 for the figures (`install.packages("ggplot2")`).
All statements and judgments here are invented for the tutorial.

## Write down what you mean

You do not need to know the right model before starting. A `claim()` can retain
an incomplete thought and the questions it leaves open.

```{r claim}
belief <- claim(
  "A longer cure may make this coating more durable.",
  author = "Tutorial researcher",
  scope = "Coating formulation F under our current preparation protocol",
  unresolved = "Does the improvement justify the extra time?"
)
record <- elicitation_record(belief)
record
```

The wording belongs to the named person. The unresolved question stays visible;
Suppose does not turn it into a numerical threshold or a probability.

## Clarify without erasing

Suppose the intended outcome is resistance to abrasion, rather than durability
in every possible sense. Create a revision and say why it changed.

```{r revise}
clearer <- revise_claim(
  belief,
  author = "Tutorial researcher",
  reason = "Specify the outcome we intend to measure",
  wording = "A longer cure may increase the number of abrasion cycles before failure.",
  target = "Mean abrasion cycles before failure",
  units = "cycles"
)
record <- record_revision(
  record,
  clearer,
  reason = "Narrow durability to the planned abrasion measurement"
)
length(record$revisions)
```

Both versions remain in the record. When the interpretation expresses your
meaning, record the review and what could challenge the belief.

```{r accept}
record <- accept_interpretation(
  record,
  author = "Tutorial researcher",
  reason = "This expresses the outcome I have in mind.",
  challenge = "Independently prepared specimens show little gain at longer cure times."
)
```

This accepts the interpretation. It does not fit a model or establish the claim.

## Add numbers when they help

`suppose_example()` supplies a separate, invented strength inquiry with two
candidate priors. The last candidate uses correlated uncertainty about the means
at 140 and 160 °C. Its judgments are about population means, not individual batches.

```{r consequences}
example <- suppose_example()
prior <- example$revisions[[3]]$candidate
prediction <- predict_prior(prior, seed = 47)
prediction
```

```{r contrast, fig.alt="Two prior distributions of strength differences. Future-batch differences are more dispersed than the uncertain population mean difference."}
plot_prior(prior, view = "contrast")
```

A future measurement varies around an uncertain mean. That extra variation
matters when you decide what to measure. The [prior consequences guide](prior-consequences.html)
works through how the assumptions produce this plot.

## Save a record you can reopen

Portable bundles are JSON data. Reopening one restores the retained objects;
it does not rerun a model or execute saved R code.

```{r save}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
write_record(record, path)
reopened <- read_record(path)
length(reopened$revisions)
```

Use a lasting path such as `"coating-inquiry.json"` for your own work.
`write_record()` refuses to overwrite an existing file unless you explicitly
request it.
